adhikaram.english: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

kurals.tamil:
அறனறிந்து மூத்த அறிவுடையார் கேண்மை
திறனறிந்து தேர்ந்து கொளல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Aranarindhu mootha arivudaiyaar kenmai
Thiranarindhu therndhu kolal.
kurals.meaning: Learn the right way to win it, weigh carefully, and then secure the friendship of those who know dharma and are mature in wisdom.
kurals.elementary: Some people know what is right and have learned a lot from long experience. This kural says: find people like that, think carefully about who they really are, and then work to make them your friends and helpers.
kurals.university: The chapter opens by fixing three qualifications for the ‘great’ (periyar): they know aram (virtue/duty), they are ‘mootha’ (ripened, whether in age or in understanding), and they possess arivu (knowledge). The verb structure is significant: ‘thiran arindhu’ (knowing the method) and ‘therndhu’ (having examined) both precede ‘kolal’ (taking). Friendship with the wise is not an accident of proximity but a deliberate, tested acquisition — a theme Valluvar develops later in the chapters on friendship (79–83). Parimelazhagar notes that this counsel is addressed first to the king, for whom advisers are an instrument of rule, but it generalises readily to anyone: one’s judgment is only as good as the judgment of those one keeps close.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Just try to learn the truth by approaching a spiritual master. Inquire from him submissively and render service unto him. The self-realized souls can impart knowledge unto you because they have seen the truth.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that real knowledge comes by deliberately approaching those who have already realized it, and by serving and questioning them with humility.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts say wisdom is gained by consciously seeking out and cultivating those who are already wise — and both specify a method (‘thiran arindhu’ / humble inquiry and service).
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong structural match; the Gita’s context is spiritual liberation, the Kural’s is practical counsel and statecraft.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs teaches that we absorb the character of those we walk with: stay close to wise people and you grow wise; keep company with fools and you share their ruin.
christianity.tie_back: Same premise as the Kural — deliberately choosing wise companions is how one gains wisdom and safety.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close in substance; Proverbs lacks the Kural’s explicit emphasis on examining before choosing.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of a good companion (who sits with you) in comparison with a bad one, is like that of the musk seller and the blacksmith’s bellows (or furnace); from the first you would either buy musk or enjoy its good smell while the bellows would either burn your clothes or your house, or you get a bad nasty smell thereof.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet compares a good companion to a perfume seller — you benefit just by being near him — and a bad companion to a blacksmith’s furnace, which harms you even if you never touch it.
islam.tie_back: Implies the same discernment the Kural demands: choose one’s companions carefully, because their quality rubs off.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified wording (sunnah.com). Hadith is about companions generally; the Kural specifies virtuous, mature and learned ones.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Appoint for thyself a teacher, and acquire for thyself a companion and judge all men with the scale weighted in his favor.”
judaism.explanation: Joshua ben Perahiah tells each person to actively make someone their teacher (asei lekha rav) and to acquire (k’neh) a companion — both are things you must go out and get.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ‘therndhu kolal’ (choose and take), the Mishnah treats a wise mentor as something one must deliberately acquire.
judaism._accuracy_note: Translation as displayed on Sefaria; very close in intent, though Avot does not specify the teacher’s age or virtue.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not to associate with the foolish, but to associate with the wise; and to honor those who are worthy of honor — this is the greatest blessing.”
buddhism.explanation: Among the Buddha’s list of the highest blessings, the very first is to avoid fools, keep company with the wise, and honor those who deserve honor.
buddhism.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s instruction to seek and honor the virtuous and wise as companions.
buddhism.source: Mangala Sutta (Khp 5 / Sn 2.4), tr. Narada Thera
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match; Narada’s wording as on Access to Insight.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Odyssey Book 2, the goddess Athena takes the form and voice of Mentor, an old and trusted friend of Odysseus, to guide the young Telemachus as he sets out to act like a man and a prince.
greek_mythology.explanation: Telemachus succeeds because he accepts guidance from an elder of proven loyalty and wisdom — so famous an image that ‘mentor’ became the word for a wise guide.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shows the Kural’s ideal: a young ruler-to-be strengthened by an aged, virtuous and knowing counselor.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Narrative parallel; Telemachus does not ‘examine and choose’ Mentor so much as accept him.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve. The process is mutual; for men learn while they teach.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca advises Lucilius to be selective about company and to seek those whose influence raises one’s own character.
philosophy.tie_back: Same deliberate selection of improving companions that the Kural commends.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 7 (tr. Gummere)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close match; Seneca adds a reciprocal element (teaching others) absent from the Kural.

adhikaram.english: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

kurals.tamil:
உற்றநோய் நீக்கி உறாஅமை முற்காக்கும்
பெற்றியார்ப் பேணிக் கொளல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Utranoi neekki uraaamai murkaakkum
Petriyaarp penik kolal.
kurals.meaning: Cherish and secure as your own those who have the ability to remove troubles that have already come and to guard you in advance against troubles yet to come.
kurals.elementary: Some wise people can help you fix a problem you already have, and can also warn you about problems before they happen. This kural says: treat people like that with great care and keep them close.
kurals.university: ‘Noi’ literally means disease, but here it stands for any affliction — political, financial, or personal. The couplet distinguishes two functions of the wise counselor: the remedial (utra noi neekki, removing the affliction already suffered) and the preventive (uraamai murkaakkum, guarding beforehand against what has not yet arrived). The latter is the rarer gift, since it requires foresight. ‘Petriyaar’ denotes those who possess this capacity as a settled quality, and ‘penik kolal’ (cherishing and holding) implies that such people must be honored and maintained, not merely consulted when convenient.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata (Adi Parva), Vidura foresees Duryodhana’s plot to burn the Pandavas in the house of lac at Varanavata; he warns Yudhishthira in a coded message and secretly sends a miner to dig an escape tunnel.
hinduism.explanation: Vidura both anticipates a danger before it strikes and provides the means of escape when it arrives, so the Pandavas survive the fire.
hinduism.tie_back: Vidura is exactly the Kural’s ‘petriyaar’: one who guards against harm before it comes and removes it when it does.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Jatugriha episode), tr. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Narrative parallel that displays both the preventive and remedial roles.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Sirs, ye should have hearkened unto me, and not have loosed from Crete, and to have gained this harm and loss.”
christianity.explanation: Paul had warned the ship’s crew not to sail; ignored, they are caught in a storm. Paul then gives the counsel that saves everyone aboard.
christianity.tie_back: Paul functions first as a preventive counselor (ignored) and then as a remedial one (heeded) — the two roles the Kural names.
christianity._accuracy_note: Illustrative narrative; the Kural’s emphasis on cherishing such people is implied rather than stated.

islam.quote_or_event: Before the Battle of the Trench (5 AH), the Prophet accepted the counsel of Salman al-Farsi to dig a defensive trench around Medina, a Persian tactic unknown to the Arabs; the besieging confederates could not break through.
islam.explanation: By heeding a knowledgeable companion, the Prophet protected the city from a danger before it arrived.
islam.tie_back: Illustrates the Kural’s ‘guarding in advance’ through valuing the counsel of a capable adviser.
islam.source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (tr. A. Guillaume)
islam._accuracy_note: Well-known sira narrative; emphasizes the preventive half of the Kural.

judaism.quote_or_event: Joseph interprets Pharaoh’s dreams and counsels him to store grain during seven years of plenty; Pharaoh appoints him over Egypt, and the land survives seven years of famine.
judaism.explanation: Joseph’s foresight lets Egypt prepare for a disaster before it arrives, and his administration carries it through when it does.
judaism.tie_back: Pharaoh ‘cherishes and holds’ the one who wards off disaster in advance — the exact wisdom of the Kural.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match for both preventive foresight and honoring the adviser.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells Sigala that a good-hearted friend who gives good counsel restrains one from doing evil, encourages one to do good, informs one of what one does not know, and points out the path to heaven.
buddhism.explanation: The true friend-counselor is defined by protecting you from wrong before it happens and guiding you toward good.
buddhism.tie_back: Parallels the Kural’s protective, forward-looking adviser who must be valued.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; concerns moral rather than worldly afflictions.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Odyssey 10, Hermes meets Odysseus on the way to Circe’s house, warns him of her drugs, and gives him the herb moly; Odysseus is protected from transformation and forces Circe to restore his men who had been turned into swine.
greek_mythology.explanation: The divine helper both forestalls the danger to Odysseus and enables the rescue of the men already afflicted.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An exact dramatization of the Kural’s two functions: removing trouble that has come, preventing trouble yet to come.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close narrative parallel; the helper is a god, not a human elder.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle writes that friendship helps the young to keep from error, and aids older people by ministering to their needs and supplementing the activities that are failing from weakness.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, friends both prevent mistakes and make up for losses already suffered.
philosophy.tie_back: Mirrors the Kural’s protective and remedial roles of the worthy companion.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.1 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Ross; Aristotle speaks of friendship generally, not of seeking superior counselors.

adhikaram.english: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

kurals.tamil:
அரியவற்று ளெல்லாம் அரிதே பெரியாரைப்
பேணித் தமராக் கொளல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ariyavatru lellaam aridhe periyaaraip
Penith thamaraak kolal.
kurals.meaning: Of all rare things, the rarest is to honor great men and make them one’s own kin.
kurals.elementary: Many things in life are hard to get. But this kural says the hardest and most precious thing of all is to have truly great people treat you like family, because you have honored and cared for them.
kurals.university: The superlative construction ‘ariyavatrul ellaam aridhe’ (rarest among all rare things) places the friendship of the great above wealth, armies, and territory, all of which are also ‘rare’ in the Porutpaal. The key word is ‘thamar’ — one’s own people, kin. Valluvar is not describing hiring an expert but transforming a great person into someone bound to you by affection and loyalty; ‘peni’ (having cherished) marks the reciprocity required. The rarity has two sources: the great are few, and they cannot be commanded — they must be won.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Satsaṅgatve nissaṅgatvaṁ, nissaṅgatve nirmohatvam; nirmohatve niścalatattvaṁ, niścalatattve jīvanmuktiḥ.”
hinduism.explanation: Shankara’s verse says that from the company of the good comes non-attachment, from that freedom from delusion, from that a steady mind, and from that liberation in this life.
hinduism.tie_back: Both treat association with the good (satsang) as the rarest and most transformative possession, the root of every higher gain.
hinduism.source: Adi Shankara (attr.), Bhaja Govindam (Moha Mudgara), verse 9
hinduism._accuracy_note: Sanskrit verse quoted in transliteration; the goal is spiritual liberation rather than worldly strength.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs says friendship must be cultivated by one’s own conduct, and that the best friend becomes closer than family.
christianity.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s ‘peni’ (cherishing) and ‘thamar’ (making them kin).
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on cultivation and kinship; Proverbs does not specify that the friend be ‘great’.

islam.quote_or_event: “And keep yourself patient [by being] with those who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening, seeking His countenance.”
islam.explanation: God tells the Prophet to hold himself firmly among the devout and not turn his eyes away from them for worldly glamour.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it values keeping close to the virtuous above worldly advantages.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified wording; the ‘rarest treasure’ framing is implied by the verse’s contrast with worldly adornment.

judaism.quote_or_event: Yose ben Yoezer taught that one’s house should be a meeting place for the sages, that one should sit in the dust of their feet and drink in their words thirstily.
judaism.explanation: Hosting and humbly attending the wise is treated as the way to fill one’s home with blessing.
judaism.tie_back: Parallels the Kural’s ideal of honoring the great and drawing them into one’s own household circle (thamar).

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Admirable friendship, admirable companionship, admirable camaraderie is actually the whole of the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: When Ananda calls good friendship ‘half’ the holy life, the Buddha corrects him: it is the whole of it.
buddhism.tie_back: The most emphatic parallel to the Kural’s claim that such friendship is the rarest of all things.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified wording on Access to Insight; spiritual rather than political context.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Odyssey 3–4, Telemachus travels to Pylos and Sparta to seek out the aged Nestor and the king Menelaus, who receive him as a guest-friend and give him counsel and news of his father.
greek_mythology.explanation: The young prince must journey to win the counsel and friendship of great elders, and is received as if family.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Reflects the rarity and value of gaining great men as one’s own.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrative; the Odyssey does not explicitly rank this above other goods.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Cherish some man of high character, and keep him ever before your eyes, living as if he were watching you, and ordering all your actions as if he beheld them.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca, quoting Epicurus, advises taking a person of high character as a constant inner companion and model.
philosophy.tie_back: Same verb of cherishing (‘peni’) applied to a great person held close.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 11 (tr. Gummere), quoting Epicurus
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close in spirit; Seneca’s ‘cherished’ figure may be absent, whereas the Kural seeks actual kinship.

adhikaram.english: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

kurals.tamil:
தம்மிற் பெரியார் தமரா ஒழுகுதல்
வன்மையு ளெல்லாந் தலை.
kurals.transliteration:
Thammir periyaar thamaraa ozhukudhal
Vanmaiyu lellaan thalai.
kurals.meaning: To conduct oneself so that those greater than oneself become one’s own is the foremost of all strengths.
kurals.elementary: Being strong isn’t just about muscles or money. This kural says the best kind of strength is behaving in a way that makes people who are wiser and better than you want to be on your side.
kurals.university: ‘Thammil periyaar’ — those greater than oneself — is the pointed phrase. Rulers and the powerful typically surround themselves with inferiors who flatter; Valluvar calls instead for the humility to keep superiors as intimates. ‘Ozhukudhal’ (conducting oneself) makes this a matter of sustained behavior, not a single act. Calling it the chief of all ‘vanmai’ (strengths) reframes power itself: the strength that multiplies other strengths is the ability to attract and retain better minds.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Before the Kurukshetra war, Arjuna and Duryodhana both come to Krishna; offered a choice between Krishna’s vast Narayani army and Krishna himself, unarmed and non-combatant, Arjuna chooses Krishna, and Duryodhana gladly takes the army.
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna values having the greater being at his side above any quantity of soldiers — and that choice decides the war.
hinduism.tie_back: A near-perfect enactment: making the one greater than oneself one’s own is the supreme strength.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.”
christianity.explanation: Friends shape and strengthen one another the way one iron blade hones another.
christianity.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s view that one’s strength is multiplied through close companions.
christianity._accuracy_note: Partial: mutual sharpening, without the Kural’s stress on seeking those greater than oneself.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with those who are true.”
islam.explanation: Believers are commanded not only to be truthful but to place themselves in the company of the truthful.
islam.tie_back: Being ‘with’ the righteous is presented as a source of spiritual strength, as the Kural presents alliance with the great.
islam._accuracy_note: Partial: the verse does not rank this above other strengths.

judaism.quote_or_event: After Honi HaMe’agel awoke from seventy years’ sleep and found no one in the study house recognized him, he prayed for death; the Talmud concludes, “O chavruta o mituta” — “either companionship or death.”
judaism.explanation: Without learned companions who know and receive him, even a great sage finds life unbearable.
judaism.tie_back: Companionship with the learned is treated as the essential strength without which life itself fails.
judaism._accuracy_note: Aramaic maxim quoted with translation; emphasizes necessity rather than seeking superiors.

buddhism.quote_or_event: After his awakening, the Buddha reflected that one who dwells without reverence and deference dwells in suffering; finding no one superior to himself, he resolved to honor and respect the Dhamma itself.
buddhism.explanation: Even the Buddha felt the need to dwell under something greater than himself.
buddhism.tie_back: Affirms the Kural’s insight that honoring and staying close to what surpasses oneself is a source of strength.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the object of reverence becomes the Dhamma, not a person.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Iliad 2, after Nestor’s advice, Agamemnon exclaims that if he had ten such counselors among the Achaeans, Priam’s city would soon fall.
greek_mythology.explanation: The supreme commander rates the counsel of the aged Nestor above multitudes of warriors.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Just as the Kural calls such alliance the chief of all strengths.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Friendship “stimulates to noble actions — ‘two going together’ — for with friends men are more able both to think and to act.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that friends increase our capacity for both thought and action.
philosophy.tie_back: Friendship as a multiplier of strength, the Kural’s central claim.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.1 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified Ross wording; Aristotle does not specify friends greater than oneself.

adhikaram.english: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

kurals.tamil:
சூழ்வார்கண் ணாக ஒழுகலான் மன்னவன்
சூழ்வாரைச் சூழ்ந்து கொளல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Soozhvaarkan naaka ozhukalaan mannavan
Soozhvaaraich soozhndhu kolal.
kurals.meaning: Since a king must conduct himself with his counselors as his eyes, he should select those counselors after careful deliberation.
kurals.elementary: A king can’t see everything himself, so his advisers are like his eyes. If your eyes are bad, you can’t see clearly. So this kural says a leader must think very carefully before choosing advisers.
kurals.university: The couplet plays on the root ‘soozh’ (to deliberate, plan): ‘soozhvaar’ are those who deliberate, and the king must ‘soozhndhu’ (deliberate) in choosing them. The wordplay enacts the argument — deliberation is needed to choose the deliberators. ‘Kan aaka’ (as eyes) is the governing metaphor: a king perceives his realm largely through ministers’ reports and judgments, so their quality determines the accuracy of his vision. The later chapter on ministers (Amaichu, ch. 64) builds on this principle.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Sovereignty (rájatva) is possible only with assistance. A single wheel can never move. Hence he shall employ ministers and hear their opinion.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya holds that no ruler can govern alone; he must appoint ministers and listen to them.
hinduism.tie_back: Same premise: the ruler depends on counselors and must choose and heed them.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified Shamasastry wording; the Arthashastra details minister selection elsewhere (1.8–1.10).

christianity.quote_or_event: “Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.”
christianity.explanation: A people whose leaders lack good counsel collapse; many sound advisers bring security.
christianity.tie_back: Affirms the ruler’s dependence on counselors that the Kural expresses.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close; lacks the Kural’s ‘eyes’ metaphor and emphasis on careful selection.

islam.quote_or_event: “… and whose affair is [determined by] consultation among themselves.”
islam.explanation: The Quran praises believers who settle their affairs by mutual consultation (shura); elsewhere (3:159) it tells the Prophet himself to consult his companions.
islam.tie_back: Consultation as a pillar of rule parallels the Kural’s ruler who sees through his counselors.
islam._accuracy_note: Shura is broader than the Kural’s selection of individual counselors.

judaism.quote_or_event: Jethro sees Moses judging the people alone from morning to evening and counsels him to choose able men, God-fearing, truthful and hating bribes, as judges over the people; Moses heeds him.
judaism.explanation: Moses accepts that a leader cannot see and judge everything himself and must select capable, upright helpers.
judaism.tie_back: Both the need for counselors and the careful criteria for choosing them echo the Kural.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match; Jethro is himself the wise counselor.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Among the conditions of welfare the Buddha gives for the Vajjian republic: they meet often in assembly, and they honor, respect, and revere their elders and deem them worthy of being listened to.
buddhism.explanation: A polity remains strong as long as it deliberates together and heeds its elders.
buddhism.tie_back: Governance through heeded counsel, as in the Kural.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a republic rather than a monarch.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Iliad 10, Diomedes, asked to pick a companion for a night raid, chooses Odysseus, observing that when two go together, one sees before the other how profit may be gained.
greek_mythology.explanation: Diomedes deliberately chooses the shrewdest partner as a second pair of eyes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Almost literally the Kural’s counselor-as-eyes chosen with care.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a military companion rather than a royal minister.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli writes that the first opinion one forms of a prince and of his understanding comes from observing the men he has around him; if they are capable and faithful, he may be reckoned wise.
philosophy.explanation: A ruler’s own wisdom is judged by the quality of the ministers he chooses.
philosophy.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s view that selecting counselors is itself the test of a ruler.
philosophy.source: Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 22 (tr. W. K. Marriott)

adhikaram.english: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

kurals.tamil:
தக்கா ரினத்தனாய்த் தானொழுக வல்லானைச்
செற்றார் செயக்கிடந்த தில்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thakkaa rinaththanaaith thaanozhuka vallaanaich
Chetraar seyakkidandha thil.
kurals.meaning: There is nothing his enemies can do to one who is able to live as a member of the company of the worthy.
kurals.elementary: If you stay close to good and wise people and act like one of them, your enemies will find there is nothing they can do to hurt you.
kurals.university: ‘Thakkaar inaththan’ — one who belongs to the fellowship of the worthy — moves from the friendship of individuals to membership in a circle. ‘Thaan ozhuka vallaan’ (one able himself to conduct himself so) implies that belonging requires one’s own discipline; the worthy will not keep company with the unworthy. The consequence is framed in the negative with total scope: ‘setraar seyak kidandhadhu il’ — there remains nothing for enemies to do. The protection is both practical (good advice closes vulnerabilities) and reputational (a ruler surrounded by the virtuous is hard to isolate).

hinduism.quote_or_event: Throughout the Mahabharata, Duryodhana’s schemes against the Pandavas — poisoning Bhima, the house of lac, the dice game and the attempt to disrobe Draupadi — repeatedly fail because the Pandavas are sheltered by Vidura’s counsel and Krishna’s friendship.
hinduism.explanation: Those who kept company with the wise and the divine proved unassailable, despite their enemies’ power.
hinduism.tie_back: Illustrates the Kural: enemies can find no effective harm to do to one who walks among the worthy.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi and Sabha Parvas (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Composite narrative illustration; the Pandavas still suffer exile, so protection is not absolute.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And if one prevail against him, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.”
christianity.explanation: Qoheleth observes that a person alone can be overpowered, but companions together withstand attack.
christianity.tie_back: Companionship as protection against enemies, as in the Kural.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on protection; does not specify that companions be ‘worthy’.

islam.quote_or_event: “… when he said to his companion, ‘Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us.’”
islam.explanation: During the Hijra, the Prophet and Abu Bakr hid in the cave of Thawr with pursuers at the entrance; the Quran recalls the Prophet reassuring his companion, and the pursuers did not find them.
islam.tie_back: The righteous companionship of the cave, under divine protection, left enemies unable to harm them.
islam._accuracy_note: Weak-to-moderate: protection is attributed to God rather than to the company of the worthy itself.

judaism.quote_or_event: Jonathan, son of King Saul, binds himself in covenant to David, warns him of Saul’s intent to kill him, and helps him escape.
judaism.explanation: David’s friendship with the righteous Jonathan shields him from a powerful enemy.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, a worthy ally renders the enemy’s designs ineffective.
judaism._accuracy_note: Narrative parallel; one friend rather than a ‘company’ of the worthy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches that monks who feel fear in lonely places should recollect the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha — the community of the noble ones — and their fear, trembling and dread will pass.
buddhism.explanation: Taking refuge in the noble community dispels fear, like soldiers who take heart looking at their commander’s banner.
buddhism.tie_back: Belonging to the worthy (the Sangha) as protection against threats — a softer, internal version of the Kural’s claim.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Weak: protection is from fear, not from external enemies’ actions.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Odyssey 22, when Odysseus fights the suitors, Athena appears at his side in the likeness of Mentor and turns aside the spears the suitors throw, so that none can harm him or his companions.
greek_mythology.explanation: The suitors, though many, can do nothing against the hero who stands with his wise ally.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Enemies find nothing they can do to one standing with the worthy.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Narrative parallel; the protector is divine.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epicurus taught that it is not so much our friends’ help that helps us as the confidence of their help.
philosophy.explanation: The assurance of trustworthy friends is itself a form of security against fortune and enemies.
philosophy.tie_back: Security through reliable, worthy friends, as in the Kural.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase (translations vary); psychological security rather than practical invulnerability.

adhikaram.english: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

kurals.tamil:
இடிக்குந் துணையாரை ஆள்வாரை யாரே
கெடுக்குந் தகைமை யவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Idikkun thunaiyaarai aalvaarai yaare
Kedukkun thakaimai yavar.
kurals.meaning: Who can ruin those who keep as companions men able to rebuke them?
kurals.elementary: A good friend will tell you when you are doing something wrong, even if it hurts to hear. This kural asks: if you keep friends like that close, who could ever bring you down?
kurals.university: ‘Idikkum’ means to strike or rebuke — Parimelazhagar glosses it as reproving the king when he errs. The couplet is a rhetorical question that assumes its answer: none. What protects the ruler is not deference but correction. The idea is especially pointed in a political treatise, since rulers are the persons least likely to hear criticism. ‘Aalvaar’ (those who rule / keep) suggests the king must actively maintain such critics in his service rather than merely tolerate them.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Sulabhāḥ puruṣā rājan satataṃ priyavādinaḥ; apriyasya ca pathyasya vaktā śrotā ca durlabhaḥ.”
hinduism.explanation: ‘O king, men who always speak pleasantly are easy to find; but one who speaks what is unpleasant yet wholesome, and one who listens to it, are hard to find.’
hinduism.tie_back: Both value the rare counselor who says what the ruler needs rather than wants to hear.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda (Maricha to Ravana); also Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Vidura Niti)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Widely cited Sanskrit verse; strong match on valuing unpleasant but beneficial counsel.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.”
christianity.explanation: A friend’s painful honesty is trustworthy; an enemy’s flattery is a trap.
christianity.tie_back: The rebuking friend as a safeguard, as in the Kural.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close; the Kural adds the claim that such friends make one unassailable.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said that the believer is the mirror of his fellow believer, and his brother who guards him against loss and protects him in his absence.
islam.explanation: A true brother shows you your faults as a mirror does and protects your interests.
islam.tie_back: The corrective companion who shields from ruin mirrors the Kural’s rebuking ally.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the hadith; ‘mirror’ implies correction rather than open rebuke.

judaism.quote_or_event: The prophet Nathan confronts King David over Bathsheba and Uriah with the parable of the poor man’s lamb, declaring “Thou art the man”; David repents, and though punished, his throne is preserved.
judaism.explanation: David keeps a prophet who dares to rebuke even the king, and his acceptance of rebuke saves his dynasty.
judaism.tie_back: A king who keeps a rebuker survives his own error — the Kural’s point exactly.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match; cf. Leviticus 19:17 on the duty to rebuke.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should one find a man who points out faults and who reproves, let him follow such a wise and sagacious person as one would a guide to hidden treasure. It is always better, and never worse, to cultivate such an association.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares a person who points out our faults to a guide who leads us to buried treasure.
buddhism.tie_back: Near-identical: the reproving companion is a treasure and a protection.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Odyssey 12, Circe warns Odysseus of the Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis; heeding her, he has his men stop their ears with wax and bind him to the mast, and passes the Sirens safely.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus survives because he accepts hard, unwelcome instructions — even about his own weakness.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Keeping and obeying a counselor who tells one hard truths keeps one from ruin.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch argues that frank speech (parrhesia) is the language of true friendship and a kind of medicine, and that the flatterer who only pleases is the greatest danger to the powerful.
philosophy.explanation: Real friends tell painful truths for our good; flatterers ruin us.
philosophy.tie_back: The same distinction between the rebuking friend and the destructive flatterer.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend (Moralia)

adhikaram.english: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

kurals.tamil:
இடிப்பாரை இல்லாத ஏமரா மன்னன்
கெடுப்பா ரிலானுங் கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Idippaarai illaadha emaraa mannan
Keduppaa rilaanung kedum.
kurals.meaning: The unguarded king who has no one to rebuke him will perish even when there is no one to destroy him.
kurals.elementary: A king with nobody brave enough to tell him he’s wrong is like someone walking without looking. Even if no enemy attacks him, he will trip over his own mistakes and fall.
kurals.university: This is the converse of 447. ‘Emaraa’ means unprotected or unsafeguarded — the missing protection is precisely the rebuker. The striking phrase ‘keduppaar ilaanum kedum’ (perishes even without destroyers) locates the source of ruin inside: unchecked error compounds until it destroys. Valluvar thus anticipates a well-known insight of political thought — that autocrats surrounded by yes-men fall by their own misjudgments more often than by foreign conquest.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Yuddha Kanda, Vibhishana urges his brother Ravana to return Sita to Rama; Ravana, surrounded by flattering ministers, insults and expels him, and Lanka is destroyed.
hinduism.explanation: Ravana drives away the one counselor willing to correct him and is ruined by his own obstinacy.
hinduism.tie_back: The king who rejects his rebuker brings about his own destruction.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match; Rama is an external destroyer, but the ruin originates in Ravana’s refusal of counsel.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy.”
christianity.explanation: One who refuses correction again and again collapses suddenly and beyond repair.
christianity.tie_back: Refusing rebuke leads to self-inflicted ruin.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close; concerns rejecting rebukers rather than lacking them.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said that the religion is sincere advice (nasihah) — to God, His Book, His Messenger, the leaders of the Muslims and their common folk.
islam.explanation: Sincere counsel to rulers is part of faith itself, implying that leaders deprived of it are endangered.
islam.tie_back: Supports the Kural’s view that a ruler needs honest advisers.
islam._accuracy_note: Partial: states the duty to advise; does not describe the fate of the unadvised.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There is yet one man, Micaiah the son of Imlah, by whom we may enquire of the LORD: but I hate him; for he doth not prophesy good concerning me, but evil.”
judaism.explanation: King Ahab prefers four hundred agreeable prophets to the one who tells him the truth; he goes to battle and is killed.
judaism.tie_back: A king who shuts out his only honest critic perishes by his own choice.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada says that the one who admonishes, instructs and shields one from wrong is dear to the good and disliked by the bad.
buddhism.explanation: Only those who are good welcome correction; those who reject the admonisher show their own ruin.
buddhism.tie_back: Implies the fate the Kural states outright for the uncorrected.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Partial; does not explicitly predict self-destruction.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Iliad 18, Polydamas urges Hector to withdraw the Trojans inside the walls now that Achilles has returned; Hector scorns him, the Trojans applaud Hector’s bad plan, and ‘no one praised Polydamas’ good counsel.’ The next day the Trojans are routed and Hector is killed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hector rejects his wise critic and brings disaster on himself and Troy.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The leader without a heeded rebuker falls through his own error.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match; Achilles is the external agent.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “A prince who is not wise himself will never take good advice.”
philosophy.explanation: In his chapter on how to avoid flatterers, Machiavelli warns that a prince surrounded by flatterers, and unable to take counsel, is ruined.
philosophy.tie_back: The ruler without honest counsel undoes himself.
philosophy.source: Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 23 (tr. W. K. Marriott)

adhikaram.english: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

kurals.tamil:
முதலிலார்க் கூதிய மில்லை மதலையாஞ்
சார்பிலார்க் கில்லை நிலை.
kurals.transliteration:
Mudhalilaark kooodhiya millai madhalaiyaanj
Chaarbilaark killai nilai.
kurals.meaning: Just as there is no profit for those without capital, there is no stability for those without the support of the worthy to prop them up.
kurals.elementary: You can’t earn money from a business if you have no money to start it. In the same way, you can’t stay steady and safe in life if you have no wise people to lean on.
kurals.university: An economic analogy fitting the Porutpaal: ‘mudhal’ (capital) is to ‘oodhiyam’ (profit) as ‘saarbu’ (support) is to ‘nilai’ (stability). ‘Madhalai’ is a prop or supporting beam — the support of the great is the load-bearing pillar of a leader’s position. The analogy implies that alliance with the worthy is not an optional extra but the principal on which all further returns are earned.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Sovereignty (rájatva) is possible only with assistance. A single wheel can never move.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya likens rule to a vehicle that cannot move on one wheel; the ruler’s helpers are the other wheel.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s prop (madhalai), assistance is the precondition of stable rule.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus compares the one who hears and does his words to a wise man who built his house on rock, which withstood the storm, and the one who does not to a foolish man who built on sand, whose house fell.
christianity.explanation: Stability depends on the foundation beneath.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, a sound support is what keeps one standing.
christianity._accuracy_note: Weak-to-moderate: the foundation is divine teaching, not wise companions.

islam.quote_or_event: “And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together and do not become divided.”
islam.explanation: The community’s stability depends on holding together to a common support.
islam.tie_back: Stability through a shared support, echoing the Kural’s ‘saarbu’.
islam._accuracy_note: Weak: the support is God’s covenant and communal unity rather than wise advisers.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up.”
judaism.explanation: Qoheleth warns that the person without companions has no one to raise him when he falls.
judaism.tie_back: Without support, there is no standing — the Kural’s ‘no stability’.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close in logic; lacks the Kural’s capital–profit analogy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha lists admirable friendship as the first prerequisite for the development of the wings to awakening, preceding virtue, right talk, persistence and discernment.
buddhism.explanation: Good friendship is the foundational capital on which all further spiritual progress is built.
buddhism.tie_back: Parallels the Kural’s ‘capital’ image: without the support of the worthy, nothing further can be gained.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The giant Antaeus was invincible while touching his mother Earth, who renewed his strength; Heracles defeated him by lifting him off the ground and crushing him in the air.
greek_mythology.explanation: Cut off from his source of support, the mightiest wrestler lost all strength.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An image of the Kural’s point: without one’s prop, there is no standing.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak-to-moderate: the support is a divine mother, not a wise counselor.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says even the rich and powerful need friends most, to preserve and use their prosperity.
philosophy.tie_back: Friends as the foundation that makes other goods stable and useful.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.1 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close; Aristotle continues that prosperity cannot be safeguarded without friends.

adhikaram.english: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

kurals.tamil:
பல்லார் பகைகொளலிற் பத்தடுத்த தீமைத்தே
நல்லார் தொடர்கை விடல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pallaar pakaikolalir paththaduththa theemaiththe
Nallaar thodarkai vidal.
kurals.meaning: To give up the friendship of the good is ten times more harmful than to incur the enmity of many.
kurals.elementary: Having lots of enemies is bad. But this kural says losing the friendship of good people is ten times worse than that.
kurals.university: The chapter closes with a calculus: ‘paththu aduththa’ (ten times over) compares two harms. Enmity from many (pallaar) is external and can be countered; abandonment of good friends (nallaar thodarkai vidal) removes the very counsel and support by which enemies are countered — so it multiplies every other danger. The verb ‘vidal’ (letting go) places responsibility on the one who drops such friendships, whether through pride, neglect, or preference for flatterers.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Stung by Vidura’s repeated advice to make peace with the Pandavas, Dhritarashtra angrily tells him to leave; Vidura goes to the Pandavas in the forest, and the king, soon realizing his loss, sends Sanjaya to bring him back.
hinduism.explanation: Casting off the one truly good counselor proves a grave loss even the king immediately feels, and the Kaurava line is later destroyed in the war he tried to prevent.
hinduism.tie_back: Forsaking the good is shown as a self-inflicted wound worse than enmity.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Narrative parallel; the ‘ten times’ comparison is implicit.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that bad company corrupts good character.
christianity.tie_back: The reverse side of the Kural: leaving good company for bad is corrosive.
christianity._accuracy_note: Weak: concerns bad company rather than the comparative harm of abandoning good friends.

islam.quote_or_event: “Oh, woe to me! I wish I had not taken that one as a friend.”
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgment, the wrongdoer bites his hands in regret for having followed a misleading friend instead of the Messenger’s way.
islam.tie_back: Abandoning the good companion for the wrong one is shown as a supreme, lasting regret.
islam._accuracy_note: Moderate: shows regret of choosing the wrong friend; no comparison with enmity.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But he forsook the counsel of the old men, which they had given him, and consulted with the young men that were grown up with him.”
judaism.explanation: Rehoboam rejects the elders who had served Solomon and follows his young peers; ten tribes break away and the kingdom is split.
judaism.tie_back: Forsaking the good counselors costs more than any external enemy could.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada advises not to associate with evil companions or seek the company of the vile, but to associate with good friends and seek the company of noble men.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha directs his followers to cling to good companions and away from bad ones.
buddhism.tie_back: Implicitly treats the loss of good friends as a serious harm, as the Kural does.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Iliad 1, Agamemnon insults Achilles and takes his prize; Achilles withdraws, and the Greeks suffer more at the Trojans’ hands than at any time in the war. In Iliad 9 Agamemnon admits his folly and offers great gifts to win him back.
greek_mythology.explanation: Alienating his best ally costs Agamemnon more than all the enemy’s efforts.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Losing the good friend is worse than the enmity of many.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good narrative parallel; Achilles is valued for strength more than counsel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “You might just as well take the sun out of the sky as friendship from life; for the immortal gods have given us nothing better or more delightful.”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius answers philosophers who advise holding friendship loosely to avoid anxiety, or seeking it only for advantage: to remove friendship from life, he says, is like removing the sun from the sky.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Cicero treats the loss of good friends as a darkness that no other good can make up for, though he does not weigh it against the enmity of many.
philosophy.source: Cicero, Laelius de Amicitia (On Friendship), §47 (ch. 13) (tr. E. S. Shuckburgh)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in the Shuckburgh translation on Project Gutenberg (eBook #2808). Strong agreement on the supreme value of friendship and the ruin of losing it; the Kural's specific 'ten times worse than the enmity of many' comparison has no counterpart in Cicero.
